title: Space Management
summary: A cushion of space around the motorcycle gives you time to react and is your best protection in a crash situation.
Keep at least a two-second following distance, measured by counting from when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed object until you reach it.
If you reach the fixed object before finishing the two-second count, you are too close and should slow down.
Use a four-second or greater gap when the area is unfamiliar, traffic is heavy, or the road is slippery.
If someone tailgates you, open up more space ahead and, when possible, change lanes to let them by.
To pass, start from the left portion of your lane at a safe following distance, check mirrors and do a head check before signaling, and move quickly through the other driver's blind spot.
After passing, check mirrors and do a head check again before signaling and returning to your lane.
When being passed, ride in the center of your lane to avoid being sideswiped, hit by debris, or pushed by wind blast.
Intersections are among the most dangerous places for riders; pick a visible lane position and assume any vehicle that could enter your path will.
When riding past parked cars, use the left portion of the lane to stay clear of opening doors, pedestrians, and cars pulling out or making U-turns.
Riding alongside another vehicle within a single marked lane is prohibited; ride in the lane center to discourage drivers from squeezing in, and do not ride between rows of stopped vehicles.
Avoid riding next to cars in adjacent lanes, and never assume merging drivers see you—give them plenty of room.

questions.q: What minimum following distance does the manual recommend under normal conditions?
options: One second
Two seconds
Three seconds
Five seconds
questions.explanation: The manual recommends the two-second rule as the baseline following distance to give extra reaction time.

questions.q: Using the two-second rule, you reach the fixed object before you finish counting "one one-thousand, two one-thousand." What should you do?
options: Maintain your speed; the count is only a guideline
Change lanes immediately
Slow down until you have more distance from the vehicle ahead
Flash your brake light at the vehicle ahead
questions.explanation: Reaching the object before the count ends means you are following too closely, so you should slow down to open the gap.

questions.q: When should a rider increase following distance to four seconds or more?
options: Only when riding with a passenger
Only at night
Whenever traveling below 30 mph
When the area is unfamiliar, traffic is heavy, or the pavement is slippery
questions.explanation: The manual calls for a four-second or larger cushion when the area is unfamiliar, traffic is congested, or the road surface is slippery.

questions.q: A vehicle is tailgating you. What does the manual recommend?
options: Tap your brakes repeatedly to warn the driver
Speed up to pull away from the vehicle
Increase your distance from the vehicle ahead and change lanes to let the driver pass when you can
Move to the right edge of the lane and stop
questions.explanation: More space ahead gives you room to handle an emergency with a tailgater behind, and changing lanes lets the driver get by safely.

questions.q: Before passing a vehicle, where in your lane should you position the motorcycle?
options: In the left portion of the lane at a safe following distance
In the right portion of the lane, close behind the vehicle
In the center of the lane, directly behind the vehicle's bumper
On the shoulder to get a better view
questions.explanation: Starting a pass from the left portion of the lane at a safe following distance makes you more visible and lets you see ahead.

questions.q: When there is enough room to pass, what should you do before signaling and accelerating into the passing lane?
options: Sound your horn
Close the gap with the vehicle ahead
Downshift two gears
Check your mirrors and do a quick head check
questions.explanation: Mirrors plus a head check let you confirm traffic behind and to the sides before you signal and move over.

questions.q: While passing another vehicle, how should you handle the driver's blind spot?
options: Slow down and match the vehicle's speed there
Pass through it quickly
Stay in it until the driver waves you by
Move to the right side of the passing lane
questions.explanation: The manual says to move quickly through the other driver's blind spot so you are not lingering where you cannot be seen.

questions.q: You have safely passed a vehicle. What should you do before returning to your original lane?
options: Use your mirrors and head checks, then signal and return
Return immediately and then signal
Brake firmly so the vehicle can see you
Wait until the passed vehicle flashes its headlights
questions.explanation: After passing, the manual calls for checking mirrors and doing head checks before signaling and moving back.

questions.q: When another vehicle is passing you, which lane position is recommended?
options: The left portion of the lane
The right portion of the lane
The center of the lane
On the shoulder
questions.explanation: Riding in the center of the lane while being passed gives a cushion of space on both sides.

questions.q: Why does riding in the center of the lane help when you are being passed by a larger vehicle?
options: It lets the passing driver use part of your lane
It reduces the risk of a sideswipe, flying debris, and wind gusts that can upset stability
It makes it easier to pass the vehicle back
It keeps you out of the oily strip in the lane
questions.explanation: The center position keeps space between you and the passing vehicle, protecting against sideswipes, debris, and wind blast from large vehicles.

questions.q: Approaching an intersection, you see a car that could pull into your path. According to the manual, what should you assume?
options: The driver has seen you and will wait
You have the right-of-way, so the car will yield
The car will turn away from you
The car will enter your path
questions.explanation: The manual advises that if a vehicle is able to enter your path at an intersection, you should assume it will.

questions.q: What should guide your lane position as you approach an intersection?
options: Choosing the position closest to the curb
Choosing the position that increases your visibility
Staying directly behind the car ahead to stay hidden
Riding on the lane line to keep both lanes open
questions.explanation: Because intersections are among the most dangerous places for riders, pick a lane position that makes you more visible to other drivers.

questions.q: When riding past a row of parked vehicles, where should you position your motorcycle?
options: In the right portion of the lane, close to the parked cars
Between the parked cars and the travel lane
Anywhere, since parked cars pose no risk
In the left portion of the lane
questions.explanation: The left portion of the lane keeps you away from opening doors, pedestrians stepping out, and cars pulling away from the curb.

questions.q: Which of these is a hazard the manual specifically mentions when passing parked vehicles?
options: Drivers or pedestrians stepping out from between vehicles
Wind blast from parked trucks
Grooved pavement near parking meters
Low-hanging tree branches
questions.explanation: The manual warns that drivers exiting their cars and pedestrians stepping between parked vehicles can cause problems, along with cars pulling out or making U-turns.

questions.q: In Massachusetts, may a motorcycle ride alongside another motor vehicle within the same marked travel lane?
options: Yes, if both drivers agree
Yes, but only in heavy traffic
No, it is prohibited
Yes, if the motorcycle stays to the right edge
questions.explanation: The manual states riders are prohibited from riding next to motor vehicles within a single marked lane, because every vehicle is entitled to the full lane.

questions.q: What lane position helps discourage drivers from trying to squeeze into your lane beside you?
options: The center of the lane
The right portion of the lane
The left portion of the lane
Directly on the lane line
questions.explanation: Riding in the center of the lane makes it harder and less tempting for a driver to share the lane with you.

questions.q: A vehicle in the next lane is traveling right beside you. What does the manual recommend?
options: Stay beside it so the driver keeps you in view
Move onto the lane line so you are more visible
Adjust your speed to open up space between you and the vehicle
Sound your horn and hold your position
questions.explanation: A car alongside may suddenly change direction into you, so change your speed until there is an adequate space cushion.

questions.q: A car is merging onto the highway near you. What is the safest approach?
options: Assume the driver sees you and hold your speed
Speed up to block the car from merging
Move to the right portion of your lane toward the car so it notices you
Do not assume the driver sees you, and give the merging vehicle plenty of space
questions.explanation: The manual warns not to assume a merging driver will notice you and advises giving entering vehicles ample room.
